title: An argument for the sake of heaven

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you argue with someone you love, what are you usually trying to do?
options: honest answer. this story is for you. listen.
then you’ll like how these two schools did it. listen.
then you’re already halfway there. listen.

steps.line: About two thousand years ago, two great teachers, Hillel and Shammai, each had a school of students. You met Hillel on day three.
Their two schools argued about many things, from Shabbat to prayer. Once, they argued for three years, each side saying, “The law follows us.”

steps.q: Three years, and no winner. Then a voice from heaven speaks. What do you think it says?
o: Both are the words of the living God
Both of you are wrong; start again
Shammai is right, but Hillel is kinder
steps.why: “These and these are the words of the living God,” and the law follows Hillel (Eruvin 13b). The rabbis call such a voice a bat kol, literally “daughter of a voice,” an echo from heaven.

steps.line: Then, the Talmud says, a voice from heaven spoke: “These and these are the words of the living God. And the law follows the school of Hillel.”

steps.q: Shammai’s school lost, yet its views are still written down. The Mishnah gives a reason for keeping losing views. What?
o: A later court might rely on them
Out of respect for Shammai himself
So no one could say they were hidden
steps.why: Mishnah Eduyot 1:5: a later court might see the reason in a losing view and rely on it. A losing argument isn’t thrown away; it waits.

steps.line: Why Hillel? Because his students were kind and humble. They taught Shammai’s view along with their own, and even taught Shammai’s first.

steps.q: Why would teaching the other side first make you more likely to be right, not just nicer?
o: You learn their weak spots to attack
You understand a view before answering it
The other side feels heard and gives in
steps.why: To teach a view first, you have to grasp it at its strongest. The Talmud says that humility is why heaven sided with Hillel (Eruvin 13b).

steps.line: And though they argued even about marriage law, the two schools still married into each other’s families. The argument never broke the friendship.

steps.q: Mishnah Avot also names an argument that was not for the sake of heaven. Whose?
o: Cain and Abel, in the field
Jacob and Esau, over the blessing
Korah and his followers, against Moses
steps.why: Avot 5:17: Hillel and Shammai argued to find the truth, and their argument lasts. Korah argued to win power, and his ended in the ground.

steps.line: Today, many Jews study in pairs, arguing over a text across a table, out loud. It isn’t a lack of faith. It’s how people learn.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. the side that lost wasn’t erased. shammai’s opinions are still written down and studied, two thousand years later.

in jewish tradition, a good argument is one for the sake of heaven: to find what’s true, not to beat someone. it’s part of why jews from different movements can disagree and still study the same pages.

steps.q: Remember the slanted mezuzah from day one? One teacher said upright, one said flat. From today’s lesson, what is the slant?
o: A mistake in how it was hung
An argument where nobody had to lose
Proof that the flat side won
steps.why: A little of both. Many Ashkenazi Jews hang it slanted, keeping both teachers on the doorpost.

today.say: next time you disagree with someone today, before you argue your side, say theirs first, as fairly as you can. that’s what hillel’s students did.
options: argue to learn, not to win. that’s your first week.
it is. that’s why it’s remembered two thousand years later.

card.keepWhy: Argue to learn, not to win.
sources: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b (three years of dispute; a heavenly voice: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows Beit Hillel; because they were kind and humble and taught Beit Shammai’s words before their own)
Mishnah Avot 5:17 (an argument for the sake of heaven will endure; Hillel and Shammai)
Mishnah Eduyot 1:5–6 (why minority opinions are recorded)
Mishnah Yevamot 1:4; Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 14b (the schools did not refrain from marrying into each other’s families)
Tosafot, Menachot 33a; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De’ah 289:6, with the Rema (the slanted mezuzah)
check: ‘About two thousand years ago’ for Hillel and Shammai (late 1st century BCE to early 1st century CE); the three-year dispute was between their schools, likely after them
